title: Injured Sea Turtle Gets a 3D-Printed Harness to Help It Swim
summary: Imagine being a sea turtle and getting hit by a boat. That's what happened to a young green sea turtle named Cebu. The boat strike hurt Cebu's spinal cord, making it hard to swim. When Cebu arrived at the Georgia Sea Turtle Center on Jekyll Island, it was very weak. At first, Cebu couldn't even swim in normal water—it had to stay in very shallow water or no water at all. As Cebu got a little stronger, the team wanted to help it exercise in deeper water. But holding a turtle all the time is stressful, and floaty devices can hurt its shell. So the team came up with a cool solution: a 3D-printed harness that floats! "We've created harnesses for other cases in the past, but Cebu needed something completely customized," says Jaynie L. Gaskin, the center's director. The harness supports Cebu while it practices using its flippers. But that's not all. Cebu is also getting stem cell therapy. Stem cells are special cells that can help repair injured tissue. It's been about a month since Cebu's second treatment, and the team is seeing encouraging changes. Cebu just had its best physical therapy session yet! Still, the turtle has a long way to go. "Cebu's prognosis remains guarded," Gaskin says. That means they're not sure if Cebu can be released back into the ocean. But for now, every little paddle is a victory.
why_it_matters: Cebu's story shows how science and caring people can help injured animals — and it reminds us that everyday choices, like boating carefully, can protect wildlife near us.

background_read: The Georgia Sea Turtle Center is a hospital for sea turtles on Jekyll Island, an island in the U.S. state of Georgia.
Green sea turtles are reptiles that live in the ocean and can grow as big as a grown-up person. They are protected because their numbers are low.
3D printing builds an object layer by layer from a computer design. It has been used to make new beaks for injured birds and shell pieces for turtles, because every animal's shape is different.
Article_Structure: WHO: Cebu, a young green sea turtle, and the team at the Georgia Sea Turtle Center
WHAT: Cebu got a custom 3D-printed floating harness plus stem cell therapy after a boat strike hurt its spinal cord
WHERE: The Georgia Sea Turtle Center on Jekyll Island
WHY: To help Cebu exercise and get stronger, though it is still not clear whether Cebu can return to the ocean

perspectives.description: The team says Cebu just had its best physical therapy session yet, and that every little paddle counts as a victory.
They describe Cebu's prognosis as 'guarded,' meaning the turtle may never be strong enough to survive back in the wild.
Some people ask whether a wild animal should live in a care center for a long time, or whether going back to the ocean should always be the goal.
